Messages.Author: Daneel
Messages.Body:
Not that it would do any good, I thought I'd just turn the tides of
flamewar back to more familiar waters with a little rantie.

[rant]

A few hours ago I had a remarkably memorable game session. I was
playing weenie Sabbat Animalism, and ousted my prey, while my grand
predator weakened my predator beyond redemption.

My grand predator was playing a fattie OBF-pre voter deck, and used
card retrieval effects like Pochtli and Reinforcements (as well as a
couple of burn option cards to speed his deck up a bit).

Since my predator was still technically in the game, I could not block
my grand-predator's PTO. I had 5 permanent intercept and superior
Animalism.

Seeing the inevitable doom, I split the Raven Spies (and one Raptor)
with Heidelberg, so it took him 3 turns to burn all my remaining
intercepty minions (after repeatedly retrieving PTO).

I was basically denied my chance to play my deck, because I did not
have AUS/SPI and was playing non-Camarilla.

After I was down to a mere shadow of my former self he ousted my
predator, me and the remaining player.

No single other card(s) could have achieved the same thing. If he had
weakened me poolwise, there would have been a risk of losing my VP.
With no minions to do my bidding, I was completely helpless. Had he
Banished my vampires, I could have easily reclaimed them (as they were
generally at capacity thanks to Hungry Coyote). Had he used combat and
(D) rushed me, I could have easily thwarted him with the aid of my
numerous retainers and some well-placed pieces of equipment (or better
yet, kicked him real hard where it hurts with my abundant Animalism
combat cards).

Mind you, I'm not pissed or anything, because the game was fun (up
till a point). I also don't mind losing, because despite the odds I
almost managed to score a 2nd VP. I also generally lose more than I
win. ;) Still, the fact that the player burned a total of about 7
non-camarilla vampires at the table with (the very same) PTO makes me
think its a powerful card; but the fact that three of those were
technically cross-table (with no chance for me to block) makes me
think it is overpowered. The apparently obvious answer (to pack more
non-intercept vote defence) seems a bit absurd, given how the only
effect that can have the same crippling effect on my play is PTO; and
I'm not sure that it is healthy for the game that I should build my
decks with allocating half a dozen cards to a specific defence against
a single (IMHO) overpowered card - just to be able to play my
(non-Camarilla) deck.

[/rant]

Best Regards,

Daneel

at least as strong as PTO's effect.
The opportunity cost isn't that hard to create and it *certainly* can
end games right when it's played. A potential 10 pool shift is certainly
going to do more to table balance than the burning of a single non-cam
vampire. Sure, you screw over one person, but Parity does the same
damned thing (as in, also screws someone), but *ALSO* nets you 5 extra
pool. Seriously, having lesser pool than ANYONE else at the table is
*not* a "weird" opportunity cost. It's a given 80% of the time and if
it's not, pool isn't really hard to get rid of.

I agree that it's sucks to be on the receiving end of a PTO when you're
playing a one-star deck, but how is it *really* different than looking
at 5 of your pool taken away and be added to someone else's pool. I have
been on the receiving end of that countless more times than I lost
vampires to PTO and I can honestly say I hate the Parity Shift more.

Mind Rape: Requires some setup to do more than just take the minion and
bleed with it. It's possible to Rape minions that can play none of the
cards in your deck, meaning you need Heidelberg, Fortitude skill cards,
or the like in order to really do some damage. Can't be directed
cross-table without the target being able to block. Starts at 0
stealth.

Form of Corruption: Takes FOREVER to kick off, even in a Free Snakes
Rant deck. Can be dealt with by ousting backwards and/or not ever
bleeding, something which is inconvenient for many decks but certainly
possible. Can only have one in play at any time. For the effect to
kick off, the minion typically must be empty or nearly so, giving the
target plenty of time to Minion Tap, Blood Doll, or otherwise use up all
of the target's blood and get some recompense for the lost minion.

Spirit Marionette: Can be dealt with by simply tapping out. Same
problems as Mind Rape; it's possible to Rape minions that can play none
of the cards in your deck, so you must have additional setup to do
damage. Is very vulnerable to intercept; Matthias can't generate THAT
much stealth, and if Kiss of Ra can affect you, then you won't get your
guy burned with Daring the Dawn.

Sure, it's dangerous to tap out every turn, and forces you to rely on
Wakes, but so does Anarch Troublemaker, Misdirection, Mind Numb, Jar the
Soul, and any of a countless number of 'tap that guy' cards.

-- Derek

target - if the bleeder is indeed your prey, bounce the bleed to your
predator (reduces pression). If it is a random cross-table bleed,
flick it towards your prey. If there is someone who has intercept,

not your predator) is doing so for rational in-game considerations and

in-game solution when selecting the target of the bounced bleed (like

(+1 1 +2 vs. +2 1 +1 +3 - that's a bleed for 4 or 7, not counting
Madman's Quill and Pentex Loves You or other bleed enhancers) you have
very depletable resources. You cannot afford to go screwin' around and
waste a bunch of good KSs on bleeding randomly. I'm not sure I have
seen many instances where someone bled backwards and still managed to

The resources you use to make someone "go away" could be used to earn
you a VP. In the vast majority of cases I choose the VP instead of
some unasserted strategic advantage. After all, most good decks will
become monsters if they have enough time. I may eliminate my extremely
dangerous grand-predator only to find me in a position where my
predator or grand-prey became unstoppable. Also where I play 2 GW is
usually enough for the Finals (heck, sometimes even 1 GW and lots of
VPs). In any given game you can fail and still compensate in the games
to come.

> > In the vast majority of cases only a poor player would bleed
> > backwards.
>
> I hope the above can bring you at least to the point where you'll admit that
> that point is debatable.

The point is (like any other point) debatable. Yet I'm still unshaken
in my stance. I'm not exactly a beginner myself, and very few times
did I see the need to bleed backwards where it mattered. Sure, I got
Theo Bell as a predator, in that case my only solution was to cycle
fast enough to get to some anti-Rush remedy. Otherwise I'm cooked in 2
turns, regardless of whether I bleed backwards or forwards. Sure, I
got another !Malk deck behind me who contested all my vamps and barely
ousts me with some random weenie. Bleeding backwards is not going to
tip the scales.

The initial cause why I assembled a !Malk deck to begin with was KS. I
hate "random" cross-table action, and like to be prepared to "punish"
it. On tournaments I usually played Malkavian Antitribu or Assamites
(because of their flexibility of applying pressure). I made finals
with both deck types, though the Assamites are too aggressive (you
sometimes have to backrush or cross-table rush preemptively, which is
not nice). I might be playing Assamites again next year, as this
year's deck is already assembled.

Note that if you are bothered with the directability of KS you are
probably an avid anti-politics lobbyman. Because things happen when
people table split. KS is only the nicer way to go; getting hammered
by (technically) unblockable Parity Shifts and KRCs cross-table is a
pain in the ass. Being bled or rushed is just so much more honest. ;)

Bye,

Daneel

In general you don't want to do pool damage to anyone except your
prey. In general other players will want to do the same thing.

There may be specific cases where someone finds strategic advantage in
causing pool damage to someone other than their prey. In those cases,
the person who is the target will likely find himself in a nonstandard
situation.

If _anyone but your prey_ bleeds you, you will generally find it
useful to bounce it towards your prey. If indeed your prey is bleeding
you, you will want to avoid the pool loss (just like when your
predator bleeds you), and you will try to gain strategic advantage
from choosing the target of the bleed well. If you cannot choose your
prey, you are in a nonstandard situation where the given circumstances
determine the best target. See the snipped paragraph about this for
details.

> KS bleeds will be for three or four, Govern bleeds will be at 5 or 6.
> KS is absolutely free, meaning you are 180 degrees off: your resources
> are hardly depletable at all.

Cards. They tend to run out if you go on going on. With 4 players, you
have at most 22.5 cards to deal with a player. Including defence,
discards, and utility cards. Assuming 4-5 cards for defence and for
discards, you are left with 15-16 cards per player. With five-card
combos that ends up being 3 packs of 5 cards.

With DEM you'll choose Kindred Spirits, Eyes of Chaos, Spying Mission,
Lost in Crowds and some random utility stealth. That's a responsible
bleed for 4 at 3 stealth. It is free and it gives you a pool if
succesful. Repeated twice, it allows you to do 4×3 or 12 pool damage
to each player - which is theoretically enough.

With DOM you'll choose Govern, Conditioning, Spying Mission, Lost in
Crowds and some random utility stealth. That's a responsible bleed for
6 at 3 stealth. It costs 2 blood and gives you nothing. But the total
damage you do is 6×3 or 18 pool.

Now... If 12 pool damage is enough to oust your prey, you'll be left
with at least a spare action that you could theoretically use to
Govern at superior, and gain 3 pool. So all in all the only difference
is the amount of blood your minions spend - which is a lot, but that
is the price of speed.

> I will choose bleeds for 3 for free and
> gaining a pool over bleeds that cost two blood for 5 *any day of the
> week*. The real determiner is deflection i.e. can you live with
> Telepathic Misdirecion and your brokenly-good bloat, or do you need the
> possibility of an untapped DOM deflector.

No. The real difference between DEM vs. DOM is not Deflection. It is
Govern the Unaligned vs. Kindred Spirits. Because, with KS you can:

1. Bleed anyone (useful, but since the prey is 99% to the left, it is
pretty cornercase)
2. Gain a pool from a succesful (!!) bleed. So much for responsible
bleeding - if you have enough stealth to make it to your prey's
reserves and you get bounced, you will have a tough choice. Gain 1
pool and get your prey 3-4 pool closer to 6 pool, or play Spying, and
forfeit the pool.
3. Free - nothing is free, of course. It does not, however, cost
blood. ;)

Whereas Govern:

1. Bleeds for +2 at inferior (at which level KS is a bleed for +0).
2. Costs a blood.
3. Can be used to put 3 blood on uncontrolled vampires. This is very
important. Which can gain you 2/3 pool if you need it at the cost of
an action that does not risk your prey getting 6 pool. That can speed
you up, possibly gaining an early action or two - which count.

DEM bleed is the reliable .44 of Stealth Bleed, whereas DOM bleed is
nothing short of an Assault Rifle.

> other person on the table, is a choice. It's a choice made by good
> players who win games. It's a choice made by players who go on to

ousted with a new predator as well. There are exceptions, but they are
just that. Generally if your predator is really the arrow to your
achilles-tendon, you'll be out before you can consider backbleeding.

> grandpredator at all is likely to result in death on the spot.

Chances are, you won't likely be hucking for nine if your predator is
really your nemesis. Nor will it be unexpected when it happens. Nor

I think a lot of this has already been discussed, so I am wary of
re-opening the topic of how to *stop* PTO. I agree that there are ways
to stop it, and that people should stop it. But I don't think this is
relevant to the issue at hand. The problem, to my mind, is that PTO is
harmful to the game in the long run.

I think that there is a power-scale from suckiness to overpowered that
most people can agree to in our heads, with slight differences. We can
all agree that Eyes of the Dead is on the sucky end of the scale. Blood
Doll is on the other end of the scale. From a player's perspective, the
difference between the two poles should not be too extreme and in fact I
would make the point that all cards should be equivalently as good as
any other card (or strive to be).

Maybe the scale can be represented like this:

Sucky/Underpowered --- So So --- Good --- Too Good/Overpowered

Reasonable cards would fall in the middle two categories.

A card designer could produce a card that says "I win. You lose. Nyah
nyah." and we would all rightfully complain because it is way to the
right of the sucky-toogood scale (See Return to Innocence). The other
end of the scale is easier to ignore, as we can all just refuse to put
cards like Tortured Confession in our decks or use them to line the
birdcage, whatever. (I just give them to new players -- my master plan
of never letting them beat me!)

There will always be some cards that are at the high end of the
spectrum, and some cards have been downgraded, such as was done with
Majesty and 5th Tradition, among others. I occasionally hear people who
disagreed with those changes, but I think the consensus is that it was
good for the game overall. Hostile Takeover went from Too Good back to
being just Good. That's fine.

At the same time, cards like Oxford University or Acquired Ventrue
Assets were brought from the Sucky end to being Usable. I approve of all
of these changes, because they narrowed the scale somewhat. It makes
more of my cards usable and that's a good thing. (LSJ -- Grand Temple of
Set needs your attention :)

This is all quite theoretical of course, not to mention that we all have
different ideas of how good or bad something is.

In my personal opinion, PTO is way outside the scale of reasonable cards
for the game. Like TOGP etc I think it needs a tone-down. In fact, I was
surprised that it didn't get one. I think PTO needed it moreso than many
cards that did get a tone-down.

I don't think this is a case of PTO being picked on because it is the
"top card" right now, as Legbiter suggested (though I agree that is a
possible problem). I don't think this is a case of mob rule either, as
Noal suggested. It is a case of a card that should never have been made
in the first place and many people are rightfully pissed that it does
exist. It either needs to be brought back down to Good or just banned
altogether. I'm happy with "Once per game" myself.

In closing, it's not so much that I am opposed to PTO specifically, so
much as that I want to maintain a reasonable scale of sucky-toogood. And
PTO (and some other cards IMO) is off that scale in a bad way. V:tES has
always had a great balance, unlike most other CCGs that I have played,
and I want to see that balance maintained.

Well, that was much longer than I thought it would be. Let the flaming
begin.

Cheers,
WES

The two are hardly equal. If you can show that the use of a given
(specialized, not staple) card allows for a significantly easier path to
victory for the user, that's a much worse problem than one which
capriciously kills an opponent's chances. The former will destroy the
diversity of the metagame as viable deck archetypes begin thinning out
to just "X" decks (using the specialized card in its specialized way)
and "anti-X" decks, which contain the specific hosers for the "X" decks.

The latter is more of "fun-ness" issue: it sucks to play a game in
which you never really had a chance due to some other players choices
of strategy. This is the problem I tend to have with rush decks, at
least when people don't win with them. They destroy their neighbors
chances of winning and then make that whole side of the table meat for
their grandpredators. You can't really ban a whole play style though,
so it's a moot point. A better example of what I'm talking about are
"Milling" or discard decks which screw the user's prey and may well
oust him but seem unlikely to get a game win very often.

The term "disruptive" that Josh used is really about how the PTO likely
hurts its victim a lot more than it helps the user. I'm sure people
can come up with a lot of examples where PTOs were used to rebalance a
game and pull someone who'd gotten ahead back down into the pack. In
the long term, though, I don't think that kind of card is good for the
game.

Fred

:) Certainly true. Many of my cards seem to qualify for that. ("Nutpunchers",

But yes, people are presumedly trying to win games as they choose the cards
they build into their decks. So the _choice_ (at least) of using a card in a
deck is a choice of a path towards victory. If they don't turn out to be that
in a given game, it's just because the metagame choice turned out to be the
wrong one.

> a 90 mummified deck is a sure loss, a 90 ascendance deck is not.

Not sure whether you're pointing out that bad cards exists or that bad
combinations of cards exist but either way, it doesn't dissuade me from
my way of looking at deckbuilding.

> The play balance effect is the cards (PTO) ability to destabilize another
> deck without a direct benefit you the person playing the PTO, unless you
> count things like Voter Cap, ect.

That's certainly a legitimate point. Just semantics. I've been calling
that "disruptiveness", for no particularly good reason except that Josh used
the word and it seemed like a good one. I've been using my definition of
"play-balance", which I believe is a popular one, for a long time.

> A
> So if we state PTO is not effective enough to win, we must therefor
> establish that the card is NOT powerful enough to make a big difference in
> game play.
>
> B
> If we state that PTO is disruptive, then we have established that the card
> is TOO powerful and makes a big difference in Play.
>
> So where do we take it. is PTO an A or B card?

Er, notice that you're using two very different definitions of the term
"power" here. For the same reason you make a distinction between "effective"
and "disruptive", you need to be careful about how you use the term
"powerful". Taking that point into account, the two statements are therefore
not mutually exclusive and I believe I agree with them both. (Also the term,
"make a big difference in game play". Again, it depends on how you define,
"make a difference".)

Fred

I would agree with you if we were splitting hair. This is not hair-
splitting, this is the crux of the matter. The words you use to describe
the difference between cards that let you win too easily and cards that
don't let you win too easily but have a devastating effect on other
players are unimportant. But it is important that you use different
words - and not confuse the matter later on down the road by fuzzing
over the mean of other words and terms: "powerful", "make a difference",
etc.

> When you have to make sub references in each sentence for each key or core
> word to define the that word and its meaning from line to line we have gone
> beyond anything useful for the General player and reader.

That's the whole point: you avoid that by agreeing on the meaning of the
words ahead of time and sticking to it. And by being aware of where you
could be about to step on a semantic land mine.

Fred
